title: Even in the Workplace, Successful Advocacy Sometimes Requires a Crowd
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The author addresses a leader whose upward advocacy for change has stalled and who must choose between giving up and raising the stakes. The proposed answer is to recruit several respected peers to make the case alongside you. A lone voice is easy to dismiss, while many voices create interest and momentum. The post adds a tactical refinement: peers usually advocate separately rather than as a bloc, since each brings a different perspective and the repeated message from multiple angles reads as more credible. A group also signals that the change is not driven by one person's self-interest.
points: When advocacy stalls, the author offers a third option beyond surrender or repetition: enlist peers.
Advocating separately, each in their own voice, is usually more persuasive than appearing as a united group.
A consistent message arriving through several lenses gains credibility with decision-makers.
Multiple advocates counter the suspicion that a proposal serves one person's self-interest.
Appearing as a group is reserved for situations closer to an intervention than to advocacy.
quotes: Change rarely begins with a crowd — but sometimes doesn’t happen without one. A single voice, no matter how passionate, is easy to dismiss.
Or you might raise the stakes by convincing several of your peers to collaborate and advocate alongside you. Peers and colleagues who stand together form a much louder voice.

Because each colleague brings a slightly different perspective, experience, and way of communicating, they typically make a stronger case by advocating separately. They don’t usually appear as a group unless the proposed change depends less on advocacy and more on an intervention.

Leaders who hear a consistent message through multiple lenses find the advocacy more credible and compelling. Better yet, a unified group of advocates signals that the proposed change does not arise from individual self-interest or from an isolated benefit.
Where one voice can begin the conversation, many voices can move it forward. Standing with multiple colleagues makes an impact. A chorus of voices is much harder for decision-makers to ignore.
